approachQuestion.prompt:
Locker divider count

Given positive N, return how many positive integers divide N exactly. Include 1 and N, counting each divisor once.

Example 1: N=36 -> 9, for 1,2,3,4,6,9,12,18,36.
Example 2: N=13 -> 2.
Example 3: N=1 -> 1.

Constraints and assumptions: 1 <= N <= 10^12. Return one count, without storing the divisors. Only exact integer arithmetic is allowed. Choose the best time bound among the offered correct methods, then the least auxiliary storage when time ties.

options.text: Test d from 1 while d<=N/d. If d divides N, add two for d and N/d, except add one when equal.
options.feedback: Every divisor below the square root has one partner above it. The equality case is the single unpaired square root.

options.text: Test every integer 1 through N and count divisors.
options.feedback: It is correct on the full domain, but tests both ends of every divisor pair individually.

options.text: Test divisors through the square root and add two for every successful test.
options.feedback: For N=36 this counts the divisor 6 twice and returns 10 rather than 9.

options.text: Return the number of divisors no greater than the square root.
options.feedback: For N=6 it returns 2 for 1,2 but omits 3,6; the answer is 4.

feedback.reason: Pair divisors around the square root and count a square root only once.
details: For d=1,2,... while d<=floor(N/d), test N mod d. A divisor contributes two unless d=N/d, when it contributes one.
A divisor d pairs with N/d. Count both except when they coincide at a perfect square. Testing d<=N/d avoids overflow in d*d while still visiting the necessary smaller member of every pair.

“Test d from 1 while d<=N/d. If d divides N, add two for d and N/d, except add one when equal.”: Every divisor below the square root has one partner above it. The equality case is the single unpaired square root.
“Test every integer 1 through N and count divisors.”: It is correct on the full domain, but tests both ends of every divisor pair individually.
“Test divisors through the square root and add two for every successful test.”: For N=36 this counts the divisor 6 twice and returns 10 rather than 9.
“Return the number of divisors no greater than the square root.”: For N=6 it returns 2 for 1,2 but omits 3,6; the answer is 4.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method (paired-divisors). Let N be the input. Choose its tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
Include initialization and any copying; no hidden preprocessing or cache.

options.text: O(log N) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Test each candidate through sqrt(N) with a fixed number of counters.
details: The loop tests floor(sqrt(N)) candidates regardless of divisibility, with constant work per candidate. A fixed number of counters is retained. Comparing d with N/d avoids squaring a potentially unsafe candidate.
Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
“O(sqrt(N)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Correct: every candidate through the square root is tested.
“O(log N) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The candidate advances by one rather than shrinking multiplicatively.
“O(N) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This is not tight for testing only the smaller member of a pair.
“O(sqrt(N)) time, O(sqrt(N)) auxiliary space”: The method counts pairs directly and saves no divisor list.
